 What’s a long walk worth? | From my Perspective
 By Doug Fitzgerald 
 Published November 2, 2026 12:00am 
 + 
 Add The Gazette on Google
 Julie Richman, Columnist 
 It’s a mighty long walk from Fort Worth, Texas to Washington, D.C. One thousand, four hundred miles to be precise. In 2016, in increments of 2.5 miles, Opal Lee began to walk the distance. Why 2.5 miles? Because it took 2.5 years for slaves in Texas to learn they were free after the Emancipation Proclamation was signed in 1863. Why undertake such a remarkable journey at the age of 89?
 Lee’s goal was to gather support for Juneteenth to become a federal holiday. Thanks to publicity and a petition signed by over 1.5 million people, her results paid off and in 2021, Juneteenth was declared a federal holiday. Juneteenth is celebrated on June 19, which marks the day in 1865 when federal troops arrived in Galveston, Texas to ensure that all enslaved people were freed. In 1979, Texas became the first state to formally recognize Juneteenth as an official holiday, but it wasn’t until 2021 that Congress passed a resolution to establish it as a federal holiday. Juneteenth honors resilience, freedom and Black history as well as the ongoing fight for equality and equal rights.

 Opal Lee was born in Texas in 1926. Her lifelong passion for activism was rooted in a childhood experience when at the age of 13, her family’s home in Galveston was destroyed by violence on the anniversary of the signing of the Emancipation Proclamation. It was June 19, 1939, when people surrounded the home, tore out the furniture, and set it on fire. That tragic day influenced the rest of her life in many ways.
 Opal Lee reacts as confetti is popped during an event honoring her 100th birthday Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, in Fort Worth, Texas. (AP Photo/Julio Cortez) 
 Opal finished college and became an educator. As a third-grade teacher, her salary was $2,000 annually so she worked a second job at an aircraft plant. After earning a master’s degree in educational counseling, Lee served as a school counselor and worked with families on issues such as truancy, connecting them with resources for food aid, medical care and housing assistance. She served on the board of directors of the county food bank and co-founded a county Black Historical and Genealogical Society.
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 After retiring from education she wrote a memoir, and her life story has been told in a children’s book and a comic book. There’s an Opal Lee Barbie and many articles about her life in textbooks and educational materials. Now, at age 100, she doesn’t walk as much as she used to, yet on October 7, 2026, she celebrated her 100th birthday with friends and supporters including Michelle Obama. That very day, construction began on the National Juneteenth Museum in Fort Worth, Texas. The museum will focus on immersive experiences, historical artifacts, and multi-media stories to illustrate Black history and the significance of Juneteenth. Opal Lee and her many descendants are looking forward to the museum’s opening. After all, she’s been the champion of the museum and is known as the grandmother of Juneteenth.
 Today, I’ll set out on a 2.5 mile walk and think of Opal Lee on her journey from Fort Worth to Washington, D.C. At 89, she clearly knew what a long walk was worth.
